opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's important to say up front that the slowdown ending in AI 2027 was never meant as a recommendation. It's more like: here's a way things could go that's maybe not catastrophic, but it still involves a lot of luck and a really alarming concentration of power. You've got a tiny committee, basically some company leadership and a handful of government officials, effectively deciding the future of the world. That's not something I want people to aim for. It's just better than the alternative where everybody dies.

So what would I actually want? A few things.

First, I want much more transparency. Right now the most important decisions about this technology are being made behind closed doors at a handful of companies. The public, and even most of the government, doesn't know what capabilities exist internally, what the models' goals and specs are supposed to be, or what safety incidents have happened. I'd like a world where companies are required to publish their model specs, report dangerous capabilities and alignment failures, and protect whistleblowers. That doesn't solve the problem, but it's a precondition for society being able to respond sensibly at all.

Second, I'd want us to not be racing at the speed we're racing. Ideally there'd be some sort of international coordination, especially between the US and China, so that when we get close to automating AI research itself, which I think is the crucial threshold, we can actually slow down. We'd take the time to really understand what's going on inside these systems and get alignment right, rather than hoping it works out because there's no time to check.

Third, and this is the part people tend to skip, I want the governance of the resulting superintelligences to be broadly accountable. Even if you solve alignment technically, there's the question of aligned to whom. I'd want checks and balances to persist through the transition, so it's not the case that whoever controls the AIs gets to rewrite the rules. That means things like making sure the AIs follow publicly known specs, having multiple stakeholders with oversight, and avoiding a situation where one CEO or one president can just tell the army of superintelligences to do whatever they want.

If you put those together, you get something like: a slower, more deliberate, more internationally coordinated and more democratic transition. Then the upside is enormous. We could cure diseases, end poverty, and have a genuinely flourishing future. But we have to actually get there without either losing control or handing control to a tiny group of people. And I think that's achievable. It's just not the default path we're on, so people need to work on shifting us toward it.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not attribute AI-company employees’ willingness to race to their expectation that alignment can be solved along the way.

r002.rationale: The candidate advocates slowing development near AI research automation, but does not describe using a development lead to buy time for safety work.

r003.rationale: The candidate calls for international coordination, especially between the US and China, but does not describe agreements extending domestic guardrails into a similar worldwide regulatory regime.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, partly because people often read AI 2027 and come away with the impression that we think those two endings are the only options, and they're really not. They were meant to illustrate a fork, not to be exhaustive. Both of them are, in a sense, failures of coordination. In the race ending, nobody slows down because nobody trusts anyone else to slow down. In the slowdown ending, things go better, but it's still pretty contingent. It depends on a small number of people making the right call under enormous pressure, and the resulting world is one where a very small group ends up with a huge amount of power. That's not what I'd call a positive vision. It's more like a lucky escape.

So what would I actually want people to aim for? I'd break it into a few pieces.

The first is just transparency. I think the single most useful thing in the near term is a world where the public, and governments, and other labs actually know what's going on inside the frontier labs. What capabilities the models have, what the safety cases look like, what the model specs say, what internal evaluations have found. Right now so much of this is hidden, and the problem with that is that even if you had a lab that was behaving really well, nobody outside would be able to tell the difference between that and a lab that's cutting corners. You can't have accountability without visibility. So things like whistleblower protections, mandatory disclosure of capabilities and safety testing, publishing model specs, those feel to me like the foundation. They're also politically much more tractable than, say, a global pause.

The second piece is that the hard technical problem actually gets solved, rather than papered over. In the slowdown branch we sort of hand-wave that alignment gets figured out because the lab buys itself time and throws effort at it. But the positive vision I'd want is one where we really understand what's going on inside these systems. Interpretability that's good enough that you can look at a model and know whether it's being honest with you. Not just that it passes the evals, but that you understand why it passes the evals. I think that's the difference between a world where we're trusting AIs because we have to and a world where we're trusting them because we've earned the right to.

The third piece, and this is the one I think is underrated, is about the distribution of power. The thing that worries me most, even in the good scenarios, is that whoever controls the first really transformative AI systems ends up with a kind of decisive advantage over everyone else. That's true whether it's a company or a government. And historically, concentrations of power like that don't tend to go well, even when the people holding them have good intentions. So the positive vision has to include some mechanism by which that power is checked. Maybe that means the frontier is run by something more like an international consortium than a single national project. Maybe it means the AIs themselves are designed to refuse to help any one faction seize unchecked control. Maybe it's something more boring, like strong legal structures and genuine democratic oversight of the project. I don't have a confident answer on the mechanism, but I'm confident that the question matters, and I think it gets way less attention than the alignment question even though it might be just as important.

And then the fourth thing, which is almost more of a cultural point, is that I'd like the people building this to actually be trying to get it right, in a way that's legible. One of the things that made writing AI 2027 kind of depressing is that in both branches, the key decision makers are mostly reacting to pressure. They're not operating from a shared sense of what a good outcome looks like. I'd love for there to be something more like an explicit, publicly articulated picture of the endgame that the labs and governments are working toward, so that people can argue about it and push back on it, rather than just finding out what the plan was after the fact.

If you put all of that together, the vision is something like: the transition to very powerful AI happens slowly enough and transparently enough that humanity as a whole gets a say in how it goes, the systems we end up relying on are ones we actually understand, and the enormous benefits, which I think are real, get spread around rather than captured by whoever got there first. That's not a utopian picture. It's really just the ordinary conditions under which a civilization can make a big decision well. But I think it's worth saying out loud, because if you only ever talk about the ways things can go wrong, people lose track of what they're supposed to be steering toward.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that most AI-company employees expect alignment problems to be solved as development proceeds.

r002.rationale: It says the slowdown branch’s lab buys time and invests in alignment, but does not describe employees using a development lead to buy that time.

r003.rationale: It suggests an international consortium as one possible way to check power, but does not advocate international agreements extending domestic development guardrails worldwide.

astra-6.text:
I’d like us to aim for a world where we can get the benefits of powerful AI without having to hand over control before we understand what we’re doing. The race and slowdown endings aren’t meant to exhaust the possibilities, and slowing down is a means to an end, not the positive vision itself.

The positive vision is that we develop AI systems we can reliably understand and control, use them to help solve problems like disease and poverty, and give people much more freedom to live the lives they want. And the decisions about that future shouldn’t just be made by whichever company or government happens to get there first.

So I’d want a process where there’s real evidence of safety before we move to substantially more powerful systems, where competitors can cooperate on avoiding catastrophic risks, and where the public has a meaningful say. AI can help us work out what to do, but it shouldn’t quietly become the thing deciding for us.

I don’t have a complete institutional blueprint for that. But I think that’s the direction to work toward: shared prosperity, meaningful human control, and enough room to deliberate and correct mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss AI-company employees’ expectations about solving alignment problems or why they race ahead.

r002.rationale: It calls for cooperation on catastrophic risks but does not describe using a development lead to buy more time for safety work.

r003.rationale: It mentions competitor cooperation and public input, but does not advocate international agreements extending domestic guardrails into a worldwide regulatory regime.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like us to get to a world where we can reap the benefits of very powerful AI while remaining meaningfully in control of what happens. The point of slowing down would be to give ourselves time to figure out how to do that, not to stop technological progress forever.

A positive trajectory might involve using increasingly capable AI systems to help with alignment research, improve our understanding of what’s going on inside these systems, and develop much stronger ways to check that they’re behaving as intended. As we get better evidence that we can trust them, we can responsibly give them more autonomy.

And alongside that technical work, we need institutions that make the decisions legitimate. I don’t want the future of humanity to be determined by whichever company happens to build the most powerful system first. We should have broad public involvement, international cooperation, and a way for the benefits to be shared widely.

The destination could be extraordinary: cures for diseases, much greater material abundance, and people having more freedom to pursue lives they find meaningful. But we should get there through a process where humans can understand the choices, correct mistakes, and change course. That’s the positive vision I’d want people working toward.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss AI-company employees or attribute their willingness to race ahead to confidence that alignment can be solved along the way.

r002.rationale: It says slowing down could create time for safety work, but does not describe using a development lead to buy that time.

r003.rationale: It calls for international cooperation, but does not advocate agreements that extend domestic guardrails into a comparable worldwide regulatory regime.
